name: Kayan neck coils

card.summary: Brass coils worn by Kayan Lahwi women that press the collarbone and ribs downward, producing a strikingly elongated neck look valued as a mark of beauty and identity.
card.note: Muscles beneath the coil weaken and skin can bruise; removal is a long process.

quick.overview:
Kayan Lahwi women of Myanmar and northern Thailand wear stacked brass coils around the neck, adding turns as they grow. The look is a very long-seeming neck, which the community regards as a mark of beauty and cultural identity.

The lengthening effect comes from the weight pushing the collarbone and ribcage down rather than the neck bones stretching. Origin theories include protection from slavery, exaggerating female slenderness, dragon symbolism and tiger-bite protection; none is confirmed.
quick.how: Girls start wearing coils from about age five, and longer coils with more turns replace them over time. Coils are rarely taken off except to be replaced.
quick.risks: Muscles under the coil weaken, and the neck and collarbone area is often bruised and discolored. Tourism in Thai villages has been controversial, and UNHCR raised concern about it in 2008.

lead: Kayan neck coils are brass rings worn by women of the Kayan Lahwi group in Myanmar and in Thai border communities. Girls begin wearing them at about age five, and coils are swapped for longer ones as turns are added over the years [1].

The effect is a neck that appears elongated, up to about 38 cm in some accounts. According to Wikipedia, the weight pushes the collarbone down and compresses the rib cage [1]. The coils function as a cultural marker of beauty and identity.

chain: Brass coils added in stages from childhood
Weight pushes collarbone and ribs downward
angle.text: The coils make the neck look much longer by lowering the collarbone line. It is a cultural beauty tradition rather than a cosmetic product.

paras: Coils are lengthened with more turns over time. Removal is a lengthy process, so coils are seldom taken off except to be replaced; the muscles under the coil weaken and the neck and collarbone area is often bruised and discolored [1].

Anthropologists have proposed several explanations: making women less attractive to other tribes to protect from enslavement, exaggerating the contrast between female and male necks, resembling a dragon from Kayan folklore, and symbolic protection from tigers. None is confirmed, and Wikipedia flags parts of this material as needing more citations [1].

Many Kayan fled conflict in Myanmar in the late 1980s and 1990s, and a long-neck area of a Thai refugee camp became a tourist attraction [1]. In January 2008 UNHCR expressed concern about tourism in these villages, and in 2006 some younger women in Mae Hong Son began removing rings to continue education or to protest exploitation of their culture [1]. Myanmar's government discouraged the rings and many women there stopped wearing them [1].

timeline.event: Some younger women in Mae Hong Son begin removing rings [1].
UNHCR voices concern over tourism in Thai long-neck villages [1].
